interactive.title: The corrector
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A short lesson in twelve small screens on one picture, the corrector. On the left is lesson 8's motor on 230 V mains, drawing 10 A while its wattmeter reads 1.6 kW, with a capacitor wired across its terminals, in parallel, so both have the full supply voltage across them. On the right is the power triangle: the true power P along the floor, 1600 W; the motor's reactive power Q_L pointing up from the end of the floor, 1652 var; and the supply's apparent power S, the long side, 2300 VA. Under the triangle, a bar shows the supply cable's current, 10 A to start with. The capacitor's slider sets its reactive power, Q_C, from 0 to 3400 var in steps of 4 var, opening at 0. Its vars are drawn as an arrow pointing down from the tip of Q_L, because a capacitor's current leads the voltage where a coil's lags, so its vars point the other way, as lesson 8's capacitor hung its triangle below the floor. The supply's triangle is what is left: its upright is Q_L − Q_C, its long side is S = √(P² + (Q_L − Q_C)²), its power factor is P ÷ S, and the supply current is S ÷ 230. P does not move, because the motor still has 230 V across it, so it still draws 10 A and takes 1600 W; the capacitor changes only what the supply has to send. Readouts give the supply current, the power factor and the capacitor's current, Q_C ÷ 230. When Q_C passes Q_L, the upright points down, the power factor readout is marked leading, and the current bar turns red as it grows again. Screen 1 starts from what Dan knows, that the fix is a capacitor in parallel, and shows how much and what it does. It opens on the motor alone: P = 1600 W, Q_L = 1652 var, S = 2300 VA, a power factor of 0.70 lagging, φ = 45.9°, and 10 A in the cable bar, as in lesson 8's puzzle. The capacitor then appears across the motor and its slider moves to 500 var: a short arrow points down from the tip of Q_L, the supply's upright shrinks to 1152 var, S to 1972 VA, and the cable bar falls to 8.57 A. Screen 2 asks what the motor's wattmeter reads now that the capacitor is fitted: 1.6 kW, unchanged; less than 1.6 kW (hint: the motor turns the same load with the same 230 V across it); or more than 1.6 kW (hint: the capacitor's power wave averages zero, as in lesson 8, so it takes no true power). A right Check slides the capacitor up and down while the floor stays at 1600 W. Screen 3 frees the slider up to 1652 var. Dragging it, the down arrow grows, the supply's upright shrinks, S shortens, the angle closes and the current bar falls. At 1000 var the upright is 652 var, S is 1728 VA, the power factor is 0.93 and the current is 7.51 A. Screen 4 asks how many vars the capacitor must supply for a power factor of 1: 1652 var, the motor's whole upright; 700 var, the gap between 2300 VA and 1600 W (hint: that gap is not a side of the triangle; the upright is); or 2300 var, the whole long side (hint: the floor, the watts, stays; only the upright is cancelled). A right Check sets 1652 var: the triangle lies flat, S = 1600 VA, the current is 1600 ÷ 230 = 6.96 A, and the cable's heat, which goes with the current squared, is (6.96 ÷ 10)² = 0.48 of what it was. Screen 5 opens the loop view: the supply, the motor and the capacitor as a small circuit, with dots for current that surge to and fro with the wave, since every current here reverses each half cycle. The motor still draws 10 A, split as in lesson 8 into its in-step part, 10 × cos 45.9° = 6.96 A, and its quarter-cycle part, 10 × sin 45.9° = 7.18 A. The capacitor's whole current is a quarter cycle out of step, so, as lesson 8's Q = V × I at 90°, it is its vars over the voltage, 1652 ÷ 230 = 7.18 A, a quarter cycle ahead of the voltage, while the motor's quarter-cycle part is a quarter cycle behind it. They are half a cycle apart, so at every instant one flows in as the other flows out, and a row of dots runs round the short loop between the capacitor and the motor while the supply cable carries only the in-step 6.96 A. Screen 6 asks what the supply cable carries, with the motor drawing 10 A and the capacitor 7.18 A: 6.96 A; 2.82 A, from 10 − 7.18 (hint: the capacitor's current cancels only the motor's quarter-cycle part, not the in-step part that does the work); or 17.18 A, the two added (hint: they are half a cycle apart, so they cancel rather than add). A right Check draws the motor's 10 A arrow, 45.9° below the floor, with the capacitor's 7.18 A arrow standing straight up from its tip, and the 6.96 A arrow that closes them lying along the floor. The triangle draws vars, where a coil's point up by convention, while these arrows draw the currents themselves, measured from the voltage, where behind is down, so the capacitor's points down in one and up in the other. Screen 7 shows the sizing in three rows that recompute as the slider moves: Q_C = Q before − Q after, where Q before is the motor's Q_L and Q after is the supply's upright you want left; X_C = V² ÷ Q_C, because the capacitor has the full 230 V across it, so its current is V ÷ X_C and its vars are V × I_C = V² ÷ X_C; and C = 1 ÷ (2πf X_C), lesson 5's rule turned round, at 50 Hz. At full correction, X_C = 230² ÷ 1652 = 32.0 Ω and C = 1 ÷ (2π × 50 × 32.0), about 99 µF. Screen 8 sets an example target power factor of 0.95 and asks how many vars the capacitor must supply: 1126 var, because the angle whose cosine is 0.95 is 18.2°, so the vars left are P × tan 18.2° = 1600 × 0.329 = 526 var, and 1652 − 526 = 1126 var; about 1570 var (hint: that is 0.95 of the motor's vars, but the power factor is a ratio of the triangle's sides, not a share of the vars to cancel); or 526 var (hint: that is what stays; the capacitor supplies the difference). A right Check sets the slider near 1126 var and fills in the rows: X_C = 47.0 Ω, C about 68 µF, and a supply current of 1600 ÷ (230 × 0.95) = 7.32 A. Screen 9 frees the slider to 3400 var. Past 1652 var the down arrow overshoots the floor, the triangle swings below the line, the power factor is marked leading, and the current bar grows again, in red. At 2500 var the upright is −848 var, S is 1811 VA, the power factor is 0.88 leading and the current is 7.87 A. Screen 10 asks what the supply cable carries if someone fits twice the capacitor, 3304 var, to be sure: about 10 A, with a power factor of 0.70 leading; 6.96 A, as low as before (hint: past full correction the capacitor's spare vars have to come along the cable too); or nearly 0 A (hint: the cable still carries the motor's in-step 6.96 A, which does the work; correction cancels only vars). A right Check sets 3304 var: the triangle is the motor's own triangle flipped below the floor, with S = 2300 VA and 10.0 A. Screens 11 and 12 are mixed. Screen 11 takes a different example load, say a compressor motor taking 3 kW and 5 kVA on 230 V, so 21.7 A, and asks for the capacitor that corrects it fully and the current after: 4 kvar and 13.0 A, from √(5² − 3²) = 4 kvar and 3000 ÷ 230 = 13.0 A; 2 kvar and 13.0 A (hint: 5 − 3 is not a side of the triangle; square, subtract, then take the square root); or 4 kvar and 4.3 A (hint: the capacitor's 17.4 A cancels only the quarter-cycle part, so it cannot be taken from 21.7 A as a plain number). A right Check draws the triangle flattening and works the capacitor: X_C = 230² ÷ 4000 = 13.2 Ω and C = 1 ÷ (2π × 50 × 13.2), about 240 µF. Screen 12 puts the first motor 20 m from its distribution board, with the capacitor drawn at the board and the loop's dots running the whole 20 m, and asks where the capacitor relieves the most cable: across the motor's terminals, so the whole run from the board carries 6.96 A; at the board, relieving the 20 m run to the motor as well (hint: the 7.18 A runs round the loop between the capacitor and the motor, so any cable inside that loop still carries the full 10 A); or anywhere, because the triangle at the supply is the same (hint: it is, but the cable between the capacitor and the motor is inside the loop). A right Check slides the capacitor to the motor's terminals, so the loop shrinks off the run. Each puzzle offers three answers; a wrong pick gets a one-line hint naming its slip, Why? explains in words, and a right Check draws the answer on the picture. The closing line says the capacitor hands the motor its vars from close by, so the supply sends only the watts' share of current, and that lesson 10 takes the same triangle to three phases.
interactive.ignores: The supply is drawn holding 230 V whatever the current; on a real installation the smaller current means a little less voltage drop, so the motor's voltage rises slightly. The capacitor is ideal and takes no true power; a real one takes a little. The motor's 1600 W and 1652 var are held fixed throughout. The waves are pure sines; a load whose current is not a sine wave needs checks this picture leaves out. The circuit is single-phase. Every current here reverses each half cycle; the dots surge to and fro with it, slowed right down, and show only where the current runs and how much, not how fast charge moves. The motors and their readings are example values.

explain.text:
A motor's current has two parts: an in-step part that does the work, and a quarter-cycle part that carries vars out to its windings and back every cycle. Fit a capacitor across the motor and it draws a current a quarter cycle the other way, so it hands the motor those vars from close by. The supply then sends only what is left, so its current falls while the motor's true power stays put. This is [[power factor correction]]: adding a load that draws reactive power the opposite way, up to an equal and opposite amount.[^3]

Start from lessons 4 and 5. The motor's quarter-cycle part lags the voltage by a quarter cycle, as lesson 4's coil did. A capacitor across the same voltage draws a current that leads it by a quarter cycle,[^4] as in lesson 5. So the two currents are half a cycle apart: whenever the motor's quarter-cycle current flows in, the capacitor's flows out, and the other way round. That is why, on the power triangle, the motor's vars, Q_L, point up and the capacitor's, Q_C, point down, and the supply sees only Q_L − Q_C. The motor barely notices: the capacitor sits beside it, not in its path, so it still has the supply's 230 V across it, still draws 10 A and still takes 1600 W. The correction does not change the load's true power.[^5] Take lesson 8's motor: 1600 W, 1652 var and 2300 VA. A capacitor of 1652 var cancels the upright completely, so the supply's apparent power drops to 1600 VA and its current to 1600 ÷ 230 = 6.96 A, from 10 A.[^5] The capacitor draws 7.18 A and the motor still draws 10 A, yet the supply carries 6.96 A, not 2.82 A or 17.18 A. Currents out of step add as arrows: the capacitor's 7.18 A cancels exactly the motor's quarter-cycle part, 10 × sin 45.9° = 7.18 A, and leaves its in-step part, 10 × cos 45.9° = 6.96 A. That 7.18 A now runs round the short loop between the capacitor and the motor instead of along the supply cable. Any power factor below 1 makes the wiring carry more current than it would with no reactance,[^6] and here the supply cable's heat, which goes with the current squared, falls to (6.96 ÷ 10)² = 0.48 of what it was.

To size the capacitor, read it off the triangle in three steps. First, the vars it must supply: Q_C = Q before − Q after. Second, its reactance: it has the full supply voltage across it, so its current is V ÷ X_C and its vars are V × I_C = V² ÷ X_C, which turns round to X_C = V² ÷ Q_C. Third, its capacitance, from lesson 5's X_C = 1/(2πfC)[^7] turned round: C = 1 ÷ (2πf X_C). For a power factor of 1 on this motor, X_C = 230² ÷ 1652 = 32.0 Ω, and at 50 Hz, C = 1 ÷ (2π × 50 × 32.0), about 99 µF. You need not go all the way. For an example target of 0.95, the angle whose cosine is 0.95 is 18.2°, so the vars left are Q after = P × tan 18.2° = 1600 × 0.329 = 526 var, and Q_C = 1652 − 526 = 1126 var. That needs 47.0 Ω, about 68 µF, and leaves 1600 ÷ (230 × 0.95) = 7.32 A in the supply.

Too much can be as bad as too little. Past 1652 var the capacitor's current outgrows the motor's quarter-cycle part, so the difference, a quarter cycle ahead of the voltage, has to come along the supply cable. The triangle swings below the floor: the power factor is now leading. Twice the capacitor, 3304 var, leaves 1652 var leading, so the supply is back to 2300 VA and 10 A, the same poor 0.70 the other way. Too much capacitance gives a low power factor just as too much inductance does,[^8] and adding more than the load's own vars is [[over-correction]]. This is a simplified model, with pure sine waves, an ideal capacitor, a steady 230 V and a motor held at one load. **A capacitor across an inductive load supplies the load's vars from close by, so, sized to Q before − Q after, it cuts the supply's current while the load's true power stays the same; too big a capacitor makes the power factor poor again, leading.[^5][^8]**

analogy.text: A winch on the front of a recovery truck draws heavy current in bursts through a long cable from the battery at the back. Fit a second battery right beside the winch and the bursts come from it, while the long cable carries only a steadier current to keep it topped up. The winch does the same work, but the long cable runs cooler. The capacitor is the battery beside the winch, the motor's vars are the bursts, and the supply cable is the long run.
analogy.breaks: The second battery evens out a demand that flows one way, from battery to winch. A motor's vars go truly out and back: each half cycle the motor hands energy to the capacitor and takes it back. And a bigger battery does no harm, where a capacitor bigger than the motor's vars sends its own to-and-fro along the supply cable.

practice.text:
- Safety first: work on a capacitor only once it is isolated and proved dead at its own terminals. It stores charge (lesson 5), so it can stay charged after the supply is switched off.
- On a single-phase load, measure the supply voltage V, the load's current I and its true power P with a wattmeter. Apparent power: S = V × I.
- The load's vars: Q before = √(S² − P²). This assumes sine-wave current; a distorted one needs more checks.
- Pick the target power factor your job sets; 0.95 below is only an example. Find the angle whose cosine it is, and Q after = P × tan of that angle. For a power factor of 1, Q after is 0.
- The capacitor's vars: Q_C = Q before − Q after.
- Its reactance: X_C = V² ÷ Q_C. Its capacitance: C = 1 ÷ (2πf X_C), at the supply's own frequency.[^7]
- Connect it across the load, in parallel, as close to the load as you can.
- Check: the motor's wattmeter reads the same, and the supply current is near P ÷ (V × target).

**Rules of thumb:** Be careful not to over-correct: keep the capacitor's vars at or below the load's own.[^8] Only the cable between the supply and the capacitor carries less; the cable from the capacitor to the load still carries the load's full current. A capacitor's vars are V² ÷ X_C = V² × 2πfC, so they go up with the frequency: one sized for 50 Hz gives 20% more vars on 60 Hz at the same voltage, and 60 Hz is the most common frequency on board ship.[^2]

**Worked example:** Lesson 8's motor on 230 V mains[^1] draws 10 A and takes 1.6 kW. S = 2300 VA, so Q before = √(2300² − 1600²) = 1652 var. For a target of 0.95, the angle is 18.2°, Q after = 1600 × 0.329 = 526 var, and Q_C = 1652 − 526 = 1126 var. X_C = 230² ÷ 1126 = 47.0 Ω, and C = 1 ÷ (2π × 50 × 47.0), about 68 µF. The supply current falls from 10 A to 1600 ÷ (230 × 0.95) = 7.32 A, while the motor still takes 1.6 kW.[^5]

**Common mistakes**
- Expecting the watts to fall. The motor does the same work; only the supply's current and volt-amps fall.[^5]
- Taking the vars as S − P, 700 var here. The upright is √(S² − P²).
- Cancelling a share of the vars, such as 0.95 × 1652. Work out what stays, P × tan φ, and supply the difference.
- Taking the capacitor's current off the load's as a plain number. It cancels only the quarter-cycle part.
- Going too big. Past the load's own vars the power factor falls again, leading.[^8]
- Fitting the capacitor at the board and expecting the load's own cable to carry less.

checks.label: UK mains electricity operates at a nominal voltage of 230V: on 230 V the motor's 10 A makes S = 2300 VA, which with its 1600 W leaves Q_L = 1652 var, a power factor of 0.70 at φ = 45.9°, and every supply current drawn is S ÷ 230

Poor power factor can be corrected, paradoxically, by adding another load to the circuit drawing an equal and opposite amount of reactive power: the capacitor's vars are drawn pointing down, the other way from the motor's, and at an equal amount the supply is left no upright and a power factor of one

This correction, of course, will not change the amount of true power consumed by the load, but it will result in a substantial reduction of apparent power, and of the total current drawn from the source: at every capacitor setting from none to the motor's whole vars, the drawn floor keeps the same true power while the drawn long side and the current bar shrink at every step

Any power factor less than 1 means that the circuit's wiring has to carry more current than what would be necessary with zero reactance: at every capacitor setting the supply current is more than P ÷ V, the in-step part, and equals it only where the upright is zero

Too much capacitance in an AC circuit will result in a low power factor just as well as too much inductance, so be careful not to over-correct: past the motor's own vars the drawn power factor falls, marked leading, and the current bar grows again in red, and twice the capacitor gives the same poor power factor, leading

Capacitive reactance can be calculated using this formula: X_C = 1/(2πfC), so turned round C = 1 ÷ (2πf X_C): with X_C = V² ÷ Q_C the sizing rows give 32.0 Ω and about 99 µF for a power factor of 1 on the motor, 47.0 Ω and about 68 µF for 0.95, and 13.2 Ω and about 240 µF for the compressor

The current leads the voltage in a capacitor: in the current arrows the capacitor's arrow stands straight up, a quarter cycle ahead of the in-step floor, while the motor's points below it, behind, and on the triangle the capacitor's vars point down, the other way from the motor's

Known answers: 500 var leaves 1152 var, 1972 VA and 8.57 A; 1000 var leaves 652 var, 1728 VA, 0.93 and 7.51 A; 2500 var gives −848 var, 1811 VA, 0.88 leading and 7.87 A; the 0.95 target needs 18.2°, tan 0.329, 526 var left and 1126 var, leaving 7.32 A; the motor splits into 6.96 A and 7.18 A; the compressor goes from 21.74 A to 13.04 A with 4 kvar and 17.39 A; the slips are 700, 2300, 2.82, 17.18, 1570 and 4.35; the cable heat falls to 0.48

Where the current goes: at full correction the drawn quarter-cycle lane in the supply cable carries nothing, while the capacitor's branch and the motor carry 7.18 A each and the in-step 6.96 A runs all round; past full correction the cable's lane runs the other way, in red; and on the last puzzle the capacitor opens at the board, its quarter-cycle lane running the whole 20 m run, and a right answer moves it to the motor's terminals, so that lane leaves the run
Each puzzle accepts only its right answer; before an answer its picture hides what is asked, a right answer draws it, and each wrong pick with a drawing draws what it claims, in red
Every demonstration has finished arriving within 4.5 s of its screen opening, none starting before the 0.35 s screen fade ends; every answer's motion, right or wrong, within 2.5 s

applied.problem: "The true power stays" reads as the supply's watts, which fall a little as cable heat drops (the lesson's own 0.48); the quote says the load's. PFC is defined as equal and opposite, yet 0.95 is partial; "too much is as bad" fails at 2500 var (0.88).

Read alone: S = V × I holds only single-phase (lesson 10 adds √3); √(S² − P²) counts only vars for sine-wave current; a motor's vars fall at light load, so a capacitor sized to full-load vars over-corrects then, against the lesson's own rule.
